records.real_world_identity_notes: Reiza's fictionalised car of the era when Formula One was moving from manual to semi-automatic gearboxes, reviewed independently of the other models in its class. Reiza's fictionalised car for the era. No real-world chassis identity is assigned, so the gearbox construction is not established beyond what the drive and the class show.
records.confidence_basis: Simulator behaviour was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the real-world transmission is supported by registered sources.
records.identity_basis: The identity is Reiza's own model name, observed exactly in live telemetry; no real-world chassis identity is assigned.
records.specification_basis: The live drive selected six H-pattern gears with no automatic cut or blip, so the driver lifts and blips. Gearbox construction is not established, so the downshift blip stays unknown.
records.confidence_notes: Guided testing directly established the gear count, the standing-start clutch, the clutchless running shifts, and the automatic cut and blip state.
control_notes: Simulator behaviour was directly observed in a guided drive in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled. There is no automatic cut or blip, so the driver lifts to upshift and blips to downshift.

Clutch telemetry was present while the running shifts were accepted as clutchless. The channel cannot separate the pedal from the clutch the car works itself, so the accepted results stand; the driver confirmed no pedal was used.

This class mixes technologies, which is period-correct. Teams adopted semi-automatic gearboxes at different times around 1990, so a manual car and a paddle car raced in the same field. Nothing is inherited between models on the strength of a shared class.

Only the high-downforce identity was observed. AMS2 selects the aero configuration from the circuit, so this car reports a different identity at a low-downforce track; that identity is not recorded here because it has not been observed and an exact match cannot be guessed.

records.specification_basis: Wikipedia gives a Weismann/McLaren longitudinal and transverse 6-speed manual, with the MP4/5B running the transverse unit, and the live drive selected six H-pattern gears with no automatic cut or blip.
records.confidence_notes: Guided testing directly established the gear count, the standing-start clutch, the clutchless running shifts, and the automatic cut and blip state.

records.real_world_identity_notes: McLaren MP4/6, the Honda RA121/E V12 car in which Ayrton Senna took the 1991 title. Wikipedia records it as the last Formula One car to win a World Championship using a manual transmission, on a Weismann/McLaren transverse six-speed manual gearbox.
records.confidence_basis: Simulator behaviour was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the real-world transmission is supported by registered sources.
records.identity_basis: A registered source establishes the MP4/6 and its manual gearbox, and the exact simulator identity was observed live.
records.specification_basis: Wikipedia gives a Weismann/McLaren transverse 6-speed manual and records the car as the last champion with a manual transmission. The live drive selected six gears with no automatic cut or blip and accepted direct gear selection, both of which agree with a manual gearbox.
records.confidence_notes: Guided testing directly established the gear count, the standing-start clutch, the clutchless running shifts, and the automatic cut and blip state.
control_notes: Simulator behaviour was directly observed in a guided drive in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled. There is no automatic cut or blip, so the driver lifts to upshift and blips to downshift.

The cockpit disagrees with itself. The visible lever and its animation are those of a sequential stick, while the gearbox accepts direct gear selection, which a sequential cannot do, and needs the driver to match revs. The mechanism is recorded as an H-pattern because that is what the gearbox does and what the real car had; the sequential-looking lever is treated as a modelling detail rather than evidence about the transmission.

The gate is recorded unknown for the same reason. A lever animated as a sequential cannot be read for a gate, and no reviewed source describes the MP4/6's shift pattern, so neither the cockpit nor the sources establish it.
Gearbox construction is not established either. The source names Weismann/McLaren but not its engagement, so the downshift blip stays unknown.

Clutch telemetry was present while the running shifts were accepted as clutchless. The channel cannot separate the pedal from the clutch the car works itself, so the accepted results stand; the driver confirmed no pedal was used.
